solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spooner’s speciality, best part’s blue?

blocks.note: the marrow of something is its pith or choicest part
sky blue; the sky is blue

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the finest bit of Spooner's party trick is a little off-colour.
explanation.walkthrough: MARROWSKY is the old name for a spoonerism, said to come from a Polish count; the 's after 'best part' is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A marrowsky is a transposition of initial sounds between words, exactly the slip associated with the Reverend William Spooner.

clue.text: Parrot largely tucked into excellent fruit

indicators.note: largely means most but not all, so the bird's name loses its final letter
something tucked into something else sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: ace means first-rate
the KEA is a New Zealand parrot, here without its last letter

explanation.surface: A greedy parrot is busy burrowing into a lovely piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The kea is a New Zealand parrot; 'largely' trims it before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The ackee is a tropical tree whose fruit is eaten in Jamaican cooking, notably with saltfish.

clue.text: Unfortunate to be choked by profligate sauce

indicators.note: being choked means being gripped round the middle, so one word is held inside the other

blocks.note: a roué is a dissolute, debauched man
ill as in ill-starred or unlucky

explanation.surface: A sorry fellow ends up strangled by a wastrel, or perhaps drowned in sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: A roué is a rake; the short word for unlucky sits inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Rouille is a garlicky, peppery Provençal sauce, usually served spread on bread with fish soup such as bouillabaisse.

clue.text: UK’s role at sea is dominant

indicators.note: being at sea means being all over the place, confused, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, the possessive S included

explanation.surface: A boast that Britain once dominated by ruling the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the surface's nod to 'Rule, Britannia!' while really signalling the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To say someone rules OK is slang graffiti for claiming they are the best, on top, holding sway over everyone else.

clue.text: Eye up silk handkerchief female’s discarded

indicators.note: something discarded is thrown away, so that letter drops out of the word

blocks.note: fogle is old thieves' slang for a silk handkerchief
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman throws away her silk hanky while someone gives her the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove F from FOGLE; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to look at someone lecherously, which is what eyeing someone up means in casual speech.

clue.text: Climber adjusting balance with rest

indicators.note: adjusting means rearranging, so the letters that follow are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mountaineer shifts their balance while taking a breather on the rock face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' looks like a mountaineer but is a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarlet bean, or scarlet runner, is a twining bean plant that climbs up poles and canes.

clue.text: Limestone pot, not small, Arabic

indicators.note: not here means without, so the letter for the next word is left out

blocks.note: skunk is a strong strain of cannabis, and pot is cannabis
S is the abbreviation for small
AR is the dictionary abbreviation for Arabic

explanation.surface: A note on an Arabic cooking pot made of limestone that isn't small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' looks like a cooking vessel but is the drug: skunk is a strong strain of cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: Kunkar is an Indian term for nodular limestone found in alluvial soils, used for lime and road-making.

clue.text: Firework display’s ending after wee bit of oafishness

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept
a bit of a word here is just its opening letter

blocks.note: wee and pee are both childish words for urine
the first letter of oafishness
the last letter of display

explanation.surface: A firework show finishes after a small spot of loutish behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' looks like Scots for small, but it is the word itself to swap; 'after' puts Y at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeoy is a Scottish homemade firework, a cone of damp gunpowder that is lit and fizzes.

clue.text: Opening time? Stay in hiding

indicators.note: the little word in goes into hiding, meaning it vanishes from the word before

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to stay is to remain

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it's opening time, and is told to stay hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening time' reads as pub hours, but 'Opening' alone is the definition; IN is dropped from REMAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A trema is a small hole or orifice, in Chambers, and also the name for a diaeresis mark.

clue.text: No gentleman to conclude I see back in the movies?

definitions.note: adjectival phrase; the answer is an adjective

indicators.note: going back means reading the whole string from right to left

blocks.note: a cit is a townsman or tradesman, contemptuously not a gentleman
amen is said to bring a prayer to its end
taken as written
C sounds like see

explanation.surface: Someone without manners finally says 'I see' and returns to watching films.
explanation.walkthrough: CIT AMEN I C, read backwards, gives CINEMATIC. 'Cit' is a Chambers word for a mere citizen.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinematic describes what belongs to or resembles film, the style of things shown on screen at the pictures.

clue.text: Search when temperature’s dropped for good shelter in Cairngorms

indicators.note: something dropped is let go, so that letter falls out of the word

blocks.note: to scout is to search around
T is the abbreviation for temperature
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Hillwalkers look for a good bothy in the Cairngorms once the temperature falls.
explanation.walkthrough: SCOUT drops its T and G replaces it. The Cairngorms are Scottish mountains, flagging a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoug is a Scots word for a shelter or sheltered place, so 'in Cairngorms' marks it as regional.

clue.text: Open University? Terribly behind with it

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly mangled, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: uni is the short form of university
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dig at the Open University for being badly out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open University' looks like one name, but 'Open' is the definition and 'University' gives UNI.
explanation.definitionFit: An uninhibited person acts freely and frankly, without reserve, which is one sense of being open.

clue.text: Charcuterie’s stocking animal organs …

indicators.note: stocking means holding in stock, so the word has the answer kept inside it

blocks.note: the letters run inside this word

explanation.surface: A delicatessen counter of cured meats keeps offal on the shelves.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to the next clue but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Uteri is the Latin plural of uterus, the womb, which is an organ of female mammals.

clue.text: … brain? Demand bovine heads removed

indicators.note: the heads of words are their first letters, and removing them strips those away

blocks.note: to ask for is to demand
a bull is a bovine animal

explanation.surface: Continuing the deli scene: a customer wants brains, ordering ox heads cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: Both ASK and BULL lose their first letters. The question mark admits the definition is loose, the case for the thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull is the bony case enclosing the brain, and colloquially stands for the head or mind itself.

clue.text: Buff liking to start with bread

indicators.note: to start with places the next piece at the very beginning, ahead of the rest

blocks.note: naan or nan is Indian flatbread
to be keen on something is to like it

explanation.surface: An enthusiast fond of beginning with a slice of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buff' looks like an enthusiast, but here it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Nankeen is a buff-coloured cotton cloth from Nanking, and the name is used for that pale yellow colour.

clue.text: Like acoustic performance that’s not advertised?

blocks.note: first meaning: a gig played without electric amplification
second meaning, read whimsically: never given a plug, never promoted

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading, splitting the word as UN-PLUGGED.
explanation.definitionFit: An acoustic set is played with instruments not connected to the mains, and a plug is a piece of publicity.

clue.text: Trying smokier nuts

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the word beside it is rearranged madly

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone attempting to roast smokier-flavoured nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying' looks like a verb, attempting, but is the adjective meaning annoying.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trying wears on your patience, which is what irksome means: tiresome and irritating.

clue.text: Hold in ring, left in flipping hooter, a little numb

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
flipping turns the whole string over so it is read from the other end
a little of a word is just a small part of it, here its opening

blocks.note: hooter is slang for the nose
L is the abbreviation for left
the first letter of numb

explanation.surface: A boxer in the ring, struck on the nose, feels it go slightly numb.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes into NOSE, N is added, then all is reversed: NOSLEN becomes NELSON. 'Flipping' also reads as a mild British curse.
explanation.definitionFit: A nelson is a wrestling hold applied from behind, arms under the opponent's armpits, used in the wrestling ring.

clue.text: Old bloodhound has carefree part of life returning to pound

indicators.note: returning means going back, so this part is read from right to left

blocks.note: L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound
May is the springtime or heyday of one's life

explanation.surface: An ageing hound remembers its carefree puppyhood and heads back to the dog pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' suggests a dogs' home, but it is the money unit's symbol, from Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyam, or lyam-hound, is an archaic name for a bloodhound, from the leash it was led on.

clue.text: Prepay hotel for relaxing mud bath treatment

indicators.note: relaxing loosens things up, so the letters are freed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Paying a spa hotel in advance to unwind with a mud bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relaxing' fits the spa picture perfectly while signalling the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelotherapy is medical treatment using mud or peat applied to the body, as in therapeutic mud baths.

clue.text: Drug addict’s first on grass (pot) leaving nothing

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the word is wanted
leaving means departing, so that letter goes out of the word

blocks.note: the first letter of addict
rice is a cereal grass
taken as written
O, zero, is nothing

explanation.surface: A junkie, high on marijuana, ends up with nothing left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' and 'pot' both look like cannabis; only 'pot' is taken literally, minus its O.
explanation.definitionFit: Aricept is a brand name for donepezil, a medicine prescribed to treat Alzheimer's disease.

clue.text: Confusion about misty rain for emmet in Cornwall?

definitions.note: emmet alone is the definition; the Cornish touch is surface play

indicators.note: about means around, so the first piece wraps round the second

blocks.note: pie, or printer's pie, is a jumbled mess of type
smir or smirr is Scots for fine drizzle

explanation.surface: Muddled weather in Cornwall, where 'emmet' is local slang for a tourist.
explanation.walkthrough: SMIR goes inside PIE. In Cornwall an emmet is a tourist, but the word's standard sense is an ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Pismire is an old or dialect word for an ant, and emmet is another archaic name for the same insect.

clue.text: Monk greeting being beset by awfully stark time

indicators.note: awfully means in a dreadful way, so the following letters are scrambled
something beset by others is surrounded by them, so it sits within

blocks.note: taken as written
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A monk's welcome is swamped by a bleak period.
explanation.walkthrough: HI sits inside the rearranged STARK TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mekhitarist is a member of an Armenian Catholic order of Benedictine monks founded by Mekhitar in 1701.

clue.text: Child, one embracing grand exodus

indicators.note: embracing means hugging, so these pieces wrap round the next one

blocks.note: an heir is a child who inherits
a means one
G is short for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: A youngster, a single one, hugging their grandparent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' is slang for a thousand pounds, abbreviated to its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hegira is Muhammad's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622, so the word means any flight or exodus.

clue.text: Excited with party hairstyle

blocks.note: up means stirred up, excited
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Thrilled to be going to a party with a new hairdo.
explanation.definitionFit: An updo is a hairstyle in which the hair is swept up and pinned on top of the head.

clue.text: Keep off level crossing right by yard

indicators.note: crossing means lying across, so the first word straddles the next

blocks.note: par means on a level, equal
R is the abbreviation for right
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A warning to keep away from the level crossing near the railway yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Level crossing' reads as one railway term, but it splits into a synonym and the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To parry a blow is to ward or fend it off, keeping an attacker at bay.

clue.text: Encampments moving guards away from the front

indicators.note: away from the front means the word loses its leading letter
moving shifts things about, so the remaining letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers breaking camp as the guards withdraw from the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: GUARDS drops G and the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A duar or douar is an Arab encampment of tents, so duars are a group of such camps.

clue.text: Water carrier’s call for silence in response

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other

blocks.note: in Chinese medicine, bi is a response of the body, a painful obstruction
hist is an old interjection demanding quiet

explanation.surface: A water seller calls for hush in reply to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water carrier' might suggest Aquarius, but here it is a person; the response comes from Chinese medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A bhisti is an Indian servant who carries water, traditionally in a goatskin bag.

clue.text: Char kept back to work during weekday

indicators.note: kept back suggests held backwards, so this piece is read right to left
during means within the span of, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: Tue is the abbreviation for Tuesday
to go is to work, as a machine does

explanation.surface: A cleaner is kept on late to work on a Tuesday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Char' looks like a cleaning lady, but it is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The togue is the North American lake trout, a large fish of the char group.

clue.text: Local bod sporting costume with finery

blocks.note: a gaud is a showy ornament, and gauds are finery
a gi or gie is the loose white suit worn for judo or karate

explanation.surface: A townsman parades in fancy dress and frills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' looks like 'wearing', but it describes the costume. GAUD comes first despite the clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaudgie, also gadgie, is a north-of-England and Scots dialect word for a man, a fellow or bloke.

clue.text: Irish sweater’s wrapper’s lost

indicators.note: a wrapper is the outer layer, so losing it strips the first and last letters

blocks.note: a jersey is a knitted sweater

explanation.surface: An Irishman's jumper has lost its packaging.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language, especially Irish Gaelic.

clue.text: I’ll pop in to present a dessert

indicators.note: popping in means dropping into a place, so the letter goes inside the word

blocks.note: to grant is to give or present
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone promising to drop by with a pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll' splits: the letter I is the fodder and 'll pop in' tells it where to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A granita is an Italian frozen dessert of coarse flavoured ice, like a grainy sorbet.

clue.text: Give up having succeeded to discharge power

indicators.note: to discharge is to let go, so that letter is dismissed from the word

blocks.note: to resign is to give up a post
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A leader quits after their successor takes power.
explanation.definitionFit: A reign is a period of rule, and the word also means sovereignty or dominion itself.

clue.text: Howler monkey blowing top?

indicators.note: blowing one's top means losing the head, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: a monkey or terror is a mischievous child

explanation.surface: A howler monkey flies into a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Howler monkey' reads as one animal, but it splits: 'Howler' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A howler is a glaring, embarrassing blunder, so it is a kind of mistake.

clue.text: Dead-head plant after early signs of spring

indicators.note: early signs are the opening letters, so only the start of the word is kept

blocks.note: the first two letters of spring
rue is a bitter herb

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: deadhead your plants once spring arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead-head' looks like a gardening job, but it is a foundry term.
explanation.definitionFit: In metal casting, a sprue or dead-head is the waste metal left in the channel through which it was poured.

clue.text: Plaster required after instrument of torture? I love contraptions!

blocks.note: gadge is an old word for an instrument of torture, or gallows
teer is an old dialect verb meaning to plaster

explanation.surface: A torture device needs a plaster cast, and its owner adores gadgets.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are obscure Chambers words; the definition is the exclamation itself, said by the person in question.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadgeteer is someone fond of inventing or using gadgets, so would exclaim a fondness for gizmos.
